content: The University of Maryland School of Medicine and the Institute of Human Virology in Nigeria collaborated with Nathan Shaffer, an independent consultant from the USA, and Annette Sohn from the Institute of HIV Research and Innovation in Thailand. Wendy Stevens from the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa, Omar Sued from Fundación Huésped in Argentina, and Daniel Were from JHPIEGO at Johns Hopkins University in the USA also contributed to this work. Evidence reviewers included Debi Boeras and Laura Broyles from the Global Health Impact Group in the USA, Rachael Burke from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine in the United Kingdom, and Caroline de Schacht from Friends in Global Health in Mozambique. Virginia Fonner from the Medical University of South Carolina in the USA, Stanzi Le Roux from the University of Cape Town in South Africa, and Robert Luo from the Global Health Impact Group in the USA also participated. Additional contributors included Peter MacPherson from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine in the United Kingdom, Andrew Phillips from University College London, Hannah Rickman from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, and Diego Silva from the University of Sydney in Australia. The overall coordination of the guideline development process was led by Nathan Ford and Marco Vitoria from the WHO Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes. They were supported by consultants Cadi Irvine and Ajay Rangaraj under the leadership of Meg Doherty, the Director of the same department. WHO headquarters staff who contributed to the development of these guidelines included Rachel Baggaley, Silvia Bertagnolio, Robin Schaefer, Philippa Easterbrook, Cheryl Johnson, David Lowrance, Virginia McDonald, Morkor Newman, Boniface Nguimfack, Martina Penazzato, Françoise Renaud, Michelle Rodolph, Andrew Seale, Satvinder Singh, Annette Verster, Lara Vojnov, and Ameyan Wole. Administrative support was provided by Dorcas Agbogla, Jasmin Leuterio, Laurent Poulain, and Mehdi Zoubedi. Budget and commissioning processes were managed by Adriana De Putter and Jerome Peron. Yann Seigenthaler, a WHO communications consultant, provided communication and product development support. David Breuer technically edited the publication, and 400 Communications Ltd handled the design and layout. WHO regional offices also contributed, with Ahmed Sabry Alaama from the Eastern Mediterranean office, Naoko Ishikawa from the Western Pacific office, Frank Lule from the Africa office, Bridget Mugisa from the Eastern Mediterranean office, Giovanni Ravasi from the Americas office, Bharat Rewari from the South-East Asia office, and Elena Vovc from the Europe office. Funding for the guideline development was provided by the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), Unitaid, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. The primary audience for this guideline includes national HIV program managers, people living with HIV, healthcare providers, and policymakers in lowand middle-income countries. It is also intended to serve as a resource for clinicians and to guide the priorities of policymakers in development agencies, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and other implementing partners. Additionally, it aims to inform people living with HIV, communities, and civil society organizations to support the implementation of updated guidance in their respective countries. The guideline update was developed following the procedures established by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The recommendations are based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which reviews evidence and formulates recommendations. WHO promotes a public health approach to scaling up testing, prevention, treatment, and care for people living with HIV in resource-limited settings. This approach aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals, including the commitment by Member States to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. In 2016, WHO updated its consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection and on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. These updates included recommendations on oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and the uptake of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in national programs, including the treat all policy, which advocates treatment for all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 cell count or clinical symptoms. Subsequent updates included recommendations for rapid ART initiation and management of advanced HIV disease in 2017, the introduction of dolutegravir (DTG) as the preferred option in first-line regimens in 2018, and its use in second-line regimens in mid-2019. Updated recommendations on infant diagnosis and HIV testing strategies were released in 2018 and 2019, respectively. The updated recommendations in this guideline address the introduction of the dapivirine vaginal ring as a new prevention option for women at substantial risk of HIV infection, the use of point-of-care technologies for infant diagnosis and treatment monitoring, and earlier initiation of ART among people with HIV and tuberculosis. These recommendations aim to optimize HIV treatment monitoring, expand prevention options, and harmonize ART for individuals co-infected with tuberculosis and those undergoing rapid ART initiation, including same-day treatment. The implementation of these recommendations within the public health approach is expected to further reduce HIV incidence and HIV-associated illness and death. WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations to these guidelines, which were developed during the COVID-19 pandemic. WHO remains committed to engaging with the global HIV community and Member States to ensure the continuity and quality of care for people living with HIV during and beyond the pandemic.
